content: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS), also known as premenstrual tension (PMT), is a condition characterized by a range of physical, psychological, and emotional symptoms that are associated with a woman’s menstrual cycle. While most women of childbearing age experience some premenstrual symptoms, PMS is specifically diagnosed when these symptoms are severe enough to interfere with daily life. These symptoms are predictable and typically occur during the luteal phase, the two weeks leading up to menstruation. Symptoms may subside once menstruation begins, but in some cases, they can persist even after bleeding starts. Irritability is a common feature of PMS, and approximately 14% of women aged 20 to 35 experience symptoms so severe that they are unable to attend work or school. In extreme cases, PMS can be disabling, and this severe form is classified as premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), which has its own psychiatric designation. Culturally, the term PMS is widely recognized in the United States and is often used colloquially to describe difficulties associated with menstruation, even in non-medical contexts. However, this casual usage often broadens the meaning beyond the clinical definition. The exact causes of PMS are not fully understood. Although PMS is linked to the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, hormone levels in affected women are typically within normal ranges. Genetic factors may play a role, as PMS appears to be more common among twins. Current research suggests that interactions between sex hormones and central nervous system neurotransmitters, particularly serotonin, may be involved. Certain medications, such as ethynodiol diacetate and ethinyl estradiol, can also contribute to PMS symptoms. There is no specific laboratory test or physical finding to confirm a diagnosis of PMS. Physicians often ask patients to keep a prospective record of their symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles to establish a pattern of premenstrual and recurring symptoms. Other conditions that could explain the symptoms must be ruled out. Standardized tools, such as the Calendar of Premenstrual Syndrome Experiences (COPE), the Prospective Record of the Impact and Severity of Menstruation (PRISM), and Visual Analogue Scales (VAS), are used to document and describe PMS. It is important to note that some medical conditions, such as depression, migraines, seizure disorders, chronic fatigue syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, asthma, and allergies, can worsen during menstruation, a phenomenon known as menstrual magnification. These conditions may mimic PMS but are not limited to the luteal phase. PMS encompasses a wide range of symptoms, with over 150 distinct symptoms identified. The severity and specific symptoms vary from person to person and from month to month. Most women with PMS experience only a subset of these symptoms. Treatment options for PMS include lifestyle modifications, dietary changes, and medical interventions. Supportive therapy, including evaluation, reassurance, and informational counseling, is an essential component of treatment to help patients regain control over their lives. Aerobic exercise has been shown in some studies to alleviate symptoms. Leading a healthy lifestyle, such as reducing caffeine, sugar, and sodium intake, increasing dietary fiber, and ensuring adequate rest and sleep, may also help. Calcium supplementation (1,200 mg/day) and vitamin E (400 IU/day) have shown some effectiveness in managing symptoms. Other suggested treatments, such as vitamin B6, magnesium, manganese, and tryptophan, lack strong evidence of efficacy. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are considered the first-line pharmacological treatment for severe PMS. Fluoxetine, at doses of 20–60 mg/day, is the most widely studied SSRI, but other options include sertraline, paroxetine, clomipramine, fluvoxamine, and nefazodone. These medications can be administered continuously or intermittently, depending on symptom recurrence. Hormonal interventions are another treatment option. Hormonal contraceptives, such as combined oral contraceptive pills and contraceptive patches, are commonly used. Progesterone support has been employed for many years, but evidence of its effectiveness is limited. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists may be effective in severe cases of PMS but are associated with significant potential side effects. Diuretics, such as spironolactone, have been used to manage water retention and have shown some benefit in studies. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, are also used to alleviate symptoms. Evening primrose oil, which contains gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), has been advocated as a treatment, but scientific evidence supporting its efficacy is lacking. Some medical professionals argue that PMS may be a socially constructed disorder. Supporters of PMS’s medical validity point to the established status of PMDD, a more severe but related condition. Studies in women with PMDD have demonstrated a correlation between self-reported emotional distress and serotonin precursor levels, as measured by positron emission tomography (PET). PMDD also has a consistent treatment response to SSRIs compared to placebos. However, proponents of the social construct theory believe that PMS and PMDD are unrelated issues, with PMDD being a product of brain chemistry and PMS being influenced by cultural and societal factors. The lack of scientifically rigorous studies on PMS contributes to the ongoing debate about its validity. Many Western studies on PMS rely on self-reporting, which may be influenced by cultural conditioning. Additionally, PMS is sometimes overdiagnosed or misdiagnosed, with other conditions, such as chronic depression or infections, being mistaken for PMS if they coincide with the premenstrual period. Critics argue that PMS is often used as a convenient explanation for emotional outbursts, even when it is not the primary cause.
